When two digits set the scale of an LTSA map

Source: vignettes/articles/ltsa-map-spread.Rmd
ltsa-map-spread.Rmd

Two of the 5,000 handwritten digits below account for 99.72% of the sum of squared distances from the center of the LTSA map. The other 4,998 are there if you zoom in. How much would you have noticed from the fraction of pixel neighbors the map retained?

What changed between the two maps?

Local Tangent Space Alignment (LTSA) fits a plane to each patch of neighboring images and finds global coordinates that align those local fits. You can keep the patches and the alignment matrix fixed and change one choice. Ordinary LTSA gives each image equal weight when it normalizes the coordinate columns. Jacobi normalization takes the weights from the diagonal of the alignment matrix. Both maps below use the same 15 images in each patch, including its center. Zhang and Zha’s LTSA paper · Jacobi normalization in flotsam

The rings mark the same 1 and 2 in both maps. Each panel shows every digit at its own map’s full range. To compare concentration independently of the axis scales, measure each image’s squared distance from its map’s centroid, then add up those distances starting with the farthest image. In ordinary LTSA the first two images already account for nearly 100%. With Jacobi normalization the top two account for 0.28%, and it takes 1,848 images to reach 90%.

Fetch the digits, fit LTSA and draw the comparison

This is the balanced training sample from the MNIST workflow. The pixel graph is exact. I build it once with 30 entries per row so you can also try a larger patch. Both 15-image fits had a connected neighborhood graph and the eigensolver reported ok.

# pak::pak(c("jlmelville/quadra", "jlmelville/snedata", "jlmelville/flotsam",
#            "jlmelville/vizier", "uwot"))
library(quadra)
digits <- snedata::download_mnist(as = "list")
train <- which(digits$meta$split == "training")
set.seed(413)
id <- sort(unlist(
  lapply(split(train, digits$meta$label[train]), sample, size = 500),
  use.names = FALSE
))
x <- digits$data[id, , drop = FALSE] / 255
label <- factor(digits$meta$label[id], levels = 0:9)
rm(digits)
graph <- rnndescent::brute_force_knn(x, k = 30, n_threads = 2)$idx
fit_ltsa <- function(k, normalize = FALSE) {
  set.seed(439)
  fit <- flotsam::ltsa(
    x,
    n_neighbors = k,
    nn_method = graph[, seq_len(k)],
    normalize = normalize,
    n_threads = 1,
    output = "result"
  )
  stopifnot(fit$eigen$status == "ok", fit$assembly$component_count == 1)
  fit$embedding
}
fits <- list(Ordinary = fit_ltsa(15), Jacobi = fit_ltsa(15, TRUE))
spread <- function(y) {
  d2 <- rowSums(scale(y, scale = FALSE)^2)
  d2 / sum(d2)
}
shares <- lapply(fits, spread)
extreme <- head(order(shares$Ordinary, decreasing = TRUE), 2)
data.frame(training_row = id[extreme], digit = label[extreme])
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(1, 0.4, 2.2, 0.4))
for (name in names(fits)) {
  y <- fits[[name]]
  vizier::embed_plot(
    y,
    colors = grDevices::hcl.colors(10, "Set 2")[label],
    title = name,
    fixed_aspect = TRUE,
    show_axes = FALSE,
    cex = 0.45
  )
  points(y[extreme, ], pch = 1, cex = 1.4, lwd = 1.5)
}
par(mar = c(3.5, 3.6, 2.2, 0.7), mgp = c(2, 0.6, 0))
curves <- vapply(
  shares,
  function(v) {
    cumsum(sort(v, decreasing = TRUE))
  },
  numeric(nrow(x))
)
cols <- c("#17638A", "#AD4E25")
matplot(
  seq_len(nrow(x)),
  100 * curves,
  type = "l",
  log = "x",
  lty = 1:2,
  lwd = 2,
  col = cols,
  xlab = "Images, farthest first",
  ylab = "Cumulative spread (%)",
  main = "Who sets the scale?"
)
legend("left", names(fits), lty = 1:2, col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n")

Can the neighbor score see the difference?

Look at the overlap column first. Both 15-image fits keep a little over one in ten of the nearest pixel neighbors. Now look at fitted-scale stress. It measures the error in the map distances after fitting the single multiplier that best matches them to the pixel distances. Zero would be a perfect fit. Even after rescaling, the ordinary map has almost as much error as setting every map distance to zero.

Fit Spread in the two farthest images Overlap at 15 Fitted-scale stress
Ordinary, 15 per patch 99.72% 0.112 0.999
Jacobi, 15 per patch 0.28% 0.119 0.622
Ordinary, 30 per patch 0.84% 0.118 0.617

The last row changes only the size of the patches used to fit ordinary LTSA. The two-point concentration all but disappears, even though I still score overlap at 15 and get much the same answer. Neighbors can keep their order in a tiny clump. Their distances tell you how much of the original geometry still fits inside it.

Do the two farthest digits also account for most of the error? Only 21 of the 20,000 sampled pairs contain either digit. Together those pairs account for 0.025% of the squared error after fitting one scale to all 20,000 pairs. Almost all the error comes from distances between images in the clump.

Measure spread, overlap and stress on the same queries and pairs

For overlap, use 100 queries per digit and all 4,999 other images as candidates. Divide the number of retained neighbors by 15 to get the fraction shared. For stress, use the same 20,000 pairs in every fit and include all their distances. Chen and Buja on neighbor overlap · Lee and colleagues on RNX · Smelser, Miller and Kobourov on scale · Takaeda’s distance-band benchmark

fits30 <- c(fits, list(Ordinary30 = fit_ltsa(30)))
set.seed(417)
audit <- sort(unlist(lapply(
  split(seq_along(label), label),
  sample,
  size = 100
)))
set.seed(415)
pairs <- sample_pairs(nrow(x), 20000)
rank15 <- exact_rank_profiles(x, fits30, k = 15, query_rows = audit)
stress <- function(ref, y, pairs) {
  random_pair_distance_band_profile(
    ref,
    y,
    bands = 1,
    pairs = pairs
  )$normalized_stress
}
scores <- lapply(names(fits30), function(name) {
  y <- fits30[[name]]
  share <- sort(spread(y), decreasing = TRUE)
  c(
    top_two_pct = 100 * sum(head(share, 2)),
    overlap = mean(rank15[[name]]$retained) / 15,
    stress = stress(x, y, pairs)
  )
})
round(do.call(rbind, setNames(scores, names(fits30))), 3)
detail <- random_pair_distance_band_profile(
  x,
  fits$Ordinary,
  bands = 1,
  pairs = pairs,
  ret_extra = TRUE
)
squared_error <- (detail$distance_in -
  detail$fitted_scale * detail$distance_out)^2
touches <- pairs[, 1] %in% extreme | pairs[, 2] %in% extreme
c(
  pairs = sum(touches),
  error_pct = 100 * sum(squared_error[touches]) / sum(squared_error)
)

Which distances should a Swiss roll preserve?

On MNIST I used one reference, Euclidean distance between pixel vectors. The Swiss roll offers two. Imagine two points directly across a fold from each other. The straight line between them can be short even when the route along the sheet is long. Fit ordinary LTSA and UMAP to the same 612 points in three dimensions, then score each map against both sets of distances. Color follows the length of the sheet from the inner turn (purple) to the outer turn (yellow).

Make the roll, fit both maps and measure stress on every pair

The Swiss-roll workflow gives the arc-length formula. Keeping arc length and height in the same units gives distances on the unrolled sheet. Both fits see only the rolled coordinates.

set.seed(63)
angle <- seq(1.5 * pi, 4.5 * pi, length.out = 2001)
arc <- (angle * sqrt(1 + angle^2) + asinh(angle)) / 2
grid <- expand.grid(
  s = seq(min(arc) + 1.5, max(arc) - 1.5, length.out = 34),
  h = seq(1, 29, length.out = 18)
)
n <- nrow(grid)
s <- grid$s + runif(n, -0.65, 0.65)
h <- grid$h + runif(n, -0.55, 0.55)
t <- approx(arc, angle, xout = s)$y
rolled <- cbind(t * cos(t), h, t * sin(t))
flat <- cbind(s, h)
ltsa <- flotsam::ltsa(
  rolled,
  n_neighbors = 15,
  nn_method = "exact",
  eig_method = "eig"
)
set.seed(414)
umap <- uwot::umap(
  rolled,
  n_neighbors = 15,
  min_dist = 0.1,
  n_threads = 1,
  n_sgd_threads = 1
)
roll_maps <- list(LTSA = ltsa, UMAP = umap)
all_pairs <- t(combn(n, 2))
round(
  sapply(list(Rolled = rolled, Unrolled = flat), function(ref) {
    vapply(
      roll_maps,
      function(y) {
        stress(ref, y, all_pairs)
      },
      numeric(1)
    )
  }),
  3
)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(0.4, 0.4, 2.3, 0.4))
views <- c(list("Unrolled sheet" = flat), roll_maps)
for (name in names(views)) {
  vizier::embed_plot(
    views[[name]],
    x = s,
    color_scheme = "grDevices::Viridis",
    title = name,
    fixed_aspect = TRUE,
    show_axes = FALSE
  )
}
Reference for fitted-scale stress LTSA UMAP
Straight through the roll (3D) 0.335 0.530
Along the unrolled sheet (2D) 0.453 0.064

If you want to read straight-line distances through the roll, LTSA has the lower stress. If you want a map of the unrolled sheet, UMAP has the lower stress by a much wider margin. I used the same maps and pairs both times. I changed which distance I wanted the map to reproduce.
